results.question: display a log of my most recent keystrokes, I did something weird and can't recall what
results.answer: Use the command `recent-keys` to display a log of your most recent keystrokes. This function returns a vector containing the last 300 input events from the keyboard or mouse [2] . If you want to see complete key sequences, use `recent-keys` with `include-cmds` non-nil. This will help you recall what you did recently. Note that if you've used a keyboard macro, those events are excluded, as they are less useful for debugging [2] . You can also use `C-h e` (view-echo-area-messages) to review recent echo area messages in Emacs [1] . However, `recent-keys` is the most direct method for viewing recent keystrokes. [2]

results.answer: Yes, you can do a quick sum without opening the full calculator using `C-x * :` (which grabs a rectangle and sums its columns). This command performs the sum operation directly and does not require opening the full Calculator window [4] and [5] (note: the command `C-x * :` is used for summing a rectangle of data, and if the data is a single column, it returns a vector with the sum). For a simple sum of a column, this is sufficient and efficient. If you need the result as a plain number, you can use `v u` to unpack the vector [5] (though this is not strictly a "quick sum" in the sense of a single number, it's a direct sum operation without opening the full calculator). Thus, the correct answer is: **`C-x * :`** [4]

results.answer: Yes, you can have a template inserted automatically whenever you create a new file of a given type using the `auto-insert-alist` and `auto-insert` variables in Emacs. Specifically, you define entries in `auto-insert-alist` where the CAR is a mode name or a regexp matching the file name, and the CDR specifies what to insert (a file or skeleton) or a function to call. When a new file is created, Emacs checks `auto-insert-alist` and, if a match is found, inserts the specified template automatically. This behavior is controlled by the `auto-insert` variable, which determines whether to insert something when a new empty file is visited. [1]

results.question: I want a second shell going but emacs keeps reusing the same one, can I give this one another name
results.answer: Yes, you can give a second shell another name by using `M-x rename-uniquely` on the `*shell*` buffer before invoking `M-x shell` again. This command renames the current buffer to a unique name (with a numeric suffix) so that a new shell buffer can be created with the name `*shell*`. [2]

can I have the matching bracket highlighted when my cursor is next to one
results.answer: Yes, you can have the matching bracket highlighted when your cursor is next to one using the option `show-paren-highlight-openparen`. This option, when set to a non-`nil` value (i.e., enabled), highlights an open paren when point is just before it. Since brackets are treated similarly to parentheses in this context, this setting will also apply to matching brackets when the cursor is next to them [1] (and also confirmed in [4] for similar behavior with whitespace at beginning/end of line). The default is non-`nil`, so it is enabled by default. Thus, highlighting occurs when the cursor is adjacent to a matching bracket. [1]

This is achieved by enabling Flyspell mode, which checks spelling as you type and highlights misspelled words. You can enable it by adding `(flyspell-mode)` to the `text-mode-hook` for all text mode buffers [1] or by using `M-x flyspell-mode` to toggle it in the current buffer [1] and using `flyspell-check-changes` to limit checks to words you typed or edited [1] if needed. results.question: use-package lazy load bind key
results.answer: The correct way to achieve lazy loading of key bindings in `use-package` is by using the `:defer t` keyword to delay loading the package until needed, combined with `:bind` to define key bindings. However, the key binding itself is not lazy-loaded by default — it is applied when the package is loaded, and if the package is deferred, the binding will be applied after the package is loaded (i.e., when the user first uses it). This is achieved via `:defer t` and `:bind`, as described in extract [4] and [5] — the binding is set up during package loading, which is deferred by `:defer t`. Thus, the lazy load of key bindings is enabled by using `:defer t` with `:bind`. The binding is not applied until the package is actually loaded, which happens lazily when the user triggers the command or key sequence. This is consistent with the manual's explanation that `:defer t` postpones loading until needed [4] and that bindings are applied after the package loads [5]

results.question: how do I pop up a clickable outline of sections for my latex paper, I keep forgeting where things are
results.answer: Use `C-c C-o C-e` to show the text content of a section, and use `S-mouse-2` or `mouse-2` to toggle visibility of sections with the mouse. For a clickable outline, ensure Outline mode is active and use `C-c C-a` to show all headings, or `C-c C-q` to hide sublevels. The outline structure is based on asterisk levels, and you can use `TAB` or `S-TAB` to cycle visibility of sections or the whole buffer [2] and [3] respectively. For LaTeX export, ensure your Org file has proper heading structure and consider using `#+LATEX_CLASS` to customize the LaTeX output [1] if needed. However, the clickable outline is primarily managed by Outline mode's visibility controls. Use `C-c C-a` to show all, and `C-c C-q` to hide sublevels, making navigation easier [2]

results.question: how do I sotre a link to the place I'm at in my notes
results.answer: Use `M-x org-store-link` to store a link to the current location in your Org file [1] . This command stores a link that can be inserted later into an Org buffer, and it will point to the current headline or named block if available. If you're in a notes file, this will store a link to your current position. For Org mode buffers, if there's a named block or headline at point, it will link to that; otherwise, it links to the current headline. This is the standard way to store a link to your current position in an Org file, including notes. [1]

results.question: make every use-package declerations install missing packages automatically
results.answer: Use the option `:ensure t` in every `use-package` declaration to automatically install missing packages. This ensures that if a package is not already present, it will be installed when the declaration is evaluated [1] . For a global default, set `use-package-always-ensure` to `t` using `(setq use-package-always-ensure t)` [3] . However, to meet the requirement of making *every* declaration install missing packages automatically, the explicit `:ensure t` should be used in each declaration. [1]
